questions.question: In the sequential formulation, why is the phrase 'for any convergent sequence' important?
options: It means one arbitrarily chosen sequence suffices for continuity
It extends the test to divergent sequences in $X$ as well
It ensures every sequence in $X$ has a convergent subsequence
One well-behaved sequence is not enough to prove continuity

questions.question: Which set-based condition is equivalent to continuity using open sets?
options: The preimage of every open set in the codomain is open in the domain.
The image of every open set in the domain is again open in the codomain.
The preimage of every open set is empty.
The image of every closed set is closed in every case.

questions.question: Which set-based condition is equivalent to continuity using closed sets?
options: The preimage of every closed set in the codomain is closed in the domain.
The image of every closed set in the domain is open in the codomain
The preimage of every closed set is the whole domain
The image of every closed set must be finite.

questions.question: Suppose $\boldsymbol{x}_i\to\boldsymbol{x}_0$ but $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_i)\to\boldsymbol{y}\ne\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)$. What follows?
options: $\boldsymbol{f}$ is continuous at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$.
$\boldsymbol{x}_i$ does not converge to $\boldsymbol{x}_0$.
$\boldsymbol{f}^{-1}$ must exist as a function.
$\boldsymbol{f}$ is not continuous at $\boldsymbol{x}_0$.

questions.question: Let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a map between metric spaces and $x_0\in X$. Which condition is the sequential characterisation of continuity of $f$ at $x_0$?
options: For every sequence $(x_i)$ in $X$ with $x_i\to x_0$, one has $f(x_i)\to f(x_0)$.
For every sequence $(x_i)$ in $X$ with $f(x_i)\to f(x_0)$, one has $x_i\to x_0$.
For every sequence $(x_i)$ in $X$ with $x_i\to x_0$, one has $f(x_i)=f(x_0)$ for all large $i$.
For every sequence $(x_i)$ in $X$ with $x_i\to x_0$, one has $d_Y(f(x_i),f(x_0))\le d_X(x_i,x_0)$ for all $i$.

questions.question: Let $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be the constant function $f(x)=1$, which is continuous, and let $V=(0,1)$. Which statement is correct?
options: $f(V)=\{1\}$ is not open, which is allowed: continuity does not constrain images of open sets.
$f(V)=\{1\}$ is not open, so the open-set criterion fails and $f$ is not continuous.
$f^{-1}(V)$ is not open, so the open-set criterion fails and $f$ is not continuous.
$f(V)=\{1\}$ is open, because a singleton is an open set in $\mathbb{R}$ with $|x-y|$.

questions.question: Let $f(x)=\tfrac{1}{x}$ on $(0,+\infty)$, which is continuous, and let $F=[1,+\infty)$, a closed set. Which statement is correct?
options: $f(F)=(0,1]$, which is not closed: continuity does not force images of closed sets to be closed.
$f(F)=[0,1]$, which is closed, as the image of a closed set under a continuous function must be.
$f(F)=(0,1]$, and this set is closed because it is the image of a closed set under a continuous $f$.
$f(F)=(0,1]$ is not closed, so $F=[1,+\infty)$ cannot be a closed set after all.

questions.question: Let $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ with $f(x)=1$ for $x>0$ and $f(x)=0$ for $x\le0$. Which sequence shows, by the sequential criterion, that $f$ is not continuous at $0$?
options: $x_i=\tfrac{1}{i}$: here $x_i\to0$ but $f(x_i)=1\not\to f(0)=0$.
$x_i=-\tfrac{1}{i}$: here $x_i\to0$ and $f(x_i)=0\to f(0)=0$.
$x_i=0$ for every $i$: here $f(x_i)=f(0)$ for every $i$.
$x_i=i$: here $f(x_i)=1$ for every $i$, while $f(0)=0$.

questions.question: Let $g\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$, $g(x,y)=x^2+y^2$, which is continuous. Which argument proves that the unit circle $S=\{(x,y)\colon x^2+y^2=1\}$ is closed?
options: $S=g^{-1}(\{1\})$ and $\{1\}$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}$, so $S$ is the preimage of a closed set under a continuous map.
$S=g^{-1}(\{1\})$ and $\{1\}$ is not open in $\mathbb{R}$, so $S$ is not open and is therefore closed.
$g(S)=\{1\}$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}$, and a continuous $g$ can only produce a closed image from a closed set.
$S=g^{-1}(\{1\})$, and preimages under a continuous map are closed whatever set $\{1\}$ is replaced by.

questions.question: Let $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous, with the usual metric $|x-y|$ on both sides, and let $B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be a set that is not open. What can be said about $f^{-1}(B)$ in general?
options: It is never open, because a preimage under a continuous map is open only when the set itself is open.
It is always closed, because $B$ is not open and the open-set criterion then makes its preimage closed.
It may be open or not open, depending on $f$ and $B$; the open-set criterion says nothing about it.
It is always open, because preimages of subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ under a continuous map are open.

questions.question: Let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a map between metric spaces such that $f^{-1}(V)$ is open in $X$ for every open $V\subseteq Y$, and let $F\subseteq Y$ be closed. Which argument shows that $f^{-1}(F)$ is closed in $X$?
options: Since $f$ maps $X\setminus f^{-1}(F)$ onto the open set $Y\setminus F$, the set $X\setminus f^{-1}(F)$ is open, so $f^{-1}(F)$ is closed.
Since $Y\setminus F$ is open, $f^{-1}(Y\setminus F)$ is open, and it equals $X\setminus f^{-1}(F)$, so $f^{-1}(F)$ is closed.
For $y_i\in F$ with $y_i\to y$, the points $f^{-1}(y_i)$ converge to $f^{-1}(y)$, so $f^{-1}(F)$ contains the limits of its sequences.
Since $Y\setminus F$ is open, $f^{-1}(Y\setminus F)$ is open, so $f^{-1}(F)$ cannot be open as well, and a set that is not open is closed.

questions.question: Let $X=(0,+\infty)$ with the metric $d(x,y)=|x-y|$, and let $f\colon X\to\mathbb{R}$, $f(x)=x^2$, which is continuous. The set $F=[-1,1]$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}$, and $f^{-1}(F)=(0,1]$. Which statement is correct?
options: $(0,1]$ is not closed in $X$, because it omits the boundary point $0$; so $f$ is not continuous on $X$ after all.
$(0,1]$ is open in $X$, because it is the complement in $X$ of the open set $f^{-1}(\mathbb{R}\setminus F)=(1,+\infty)$.
$f^{-1}(F)$ is really $[-1,1]$, the solution set of $x^2\le1$, and this set is closed, as the criterion requires.
$(0,1]$ is closed in $X$: since $0\notin X$, its only boundary point in $X$ is $1$, which belongs to it.
